clue.text: Dedication not so much in evidence in a crooner

indicators.note: the phrase says one word sits visibly within the singer's name

parts.note: Bing Crosby is the archetypal crooner
not so much means less

explanation.surface: A singer whose commitment is barely noticeable.
explanation.definitionFit: A dedication, as of a church or a meal, is a consecration or grace asking divine favour.

clue.text: Dispatch article supporting ambassador in retirement

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the word for retirement

parts.note: going to bed is retiring for the night

indicators.note: in a down clue a piece supporting another sits beneath it, so it follows

parts.note: HE, His Excellency, is the style of an ambassador
A is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A news report about an ambassador who has stepped down from service.
explanation.walkthrough: The OCR gave 'recrement'; the page prints 'retirement'. In a down clue 'supporting' means placed below, so the article follows the ambassador; 'in' puts the pair inside the word for retirement.
explanation.definitionFit: To dispatch someone is to kill them, and cutting off the head is one way to execute.

clue.text: Foxhole to act as part of the defence

parts.note: a fox's den is called its earth
to act or function is to work

explanation.surface: A soldier's foxhole doing duty in the line of defence.
explanation.definitionFit: An earthwork is a bank or rampart of soil built as a military fortification.

clue.text: Tom's sayings about the old river?

definitions.note: possessive: Tom Sawyer's, read as the plural surname

indicators.note: the word for sayings goes round the other letters

parts.note: saws are proverbs or sayings
ye is the old form of the

explanation.surface: Mark Twain's hero Tom spouting proverbs about the old Mississippi.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom Sawyer is Mark Twain's boy hero who lives by the Mississippi; the definition reads 'Tom's' as SAWYER'S, which shares its letters with the plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Tom Sawyer is Mark Twain's hero, so his possessions are the Sawyer's.

clue.text: Dash up to see detailed tender

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: to dash is to run

explanation.surface: Hurrying to check on a carefully specified offer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dash up' turns RUN into NUR; 'detailed' is read as de-tailed, so SEE loses its last E to give SE.
explanation.definitionFit: To tend a patient is to nurse them; a tender is a carer.

clue.text: Edison's 99% perspiratory condition

parts.note: Thomas Edison's famous saying put it down as one per cent inspiration and ninety-nine per cent perspiration

explanation.surface: The inventor's state of being mostly sweat.
explanation.definitionFit: Edison famously defined exceptional brilliance as largely hard work and sweat.

clue.text: Choose a sound member of Uncle Sam's college?

definitions.text: Choose a sound member of Uncle Sam's college?

parts.words: Choose a sound member of Uncle Sam's college?
parts.note: one who chooses a sound candidate, and a member of the US ... College that picks the president

explanation.surface: Advice on picking a good candidate for an American university.
explanation.walkthrough: The US president is chosen by the Electoral College; each of its members is one who elects, so the clue's 'Choose' sits inside the answer's sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A voter in America's Electoral College casts a ballot for the president.

clue.text: Observed one employed in gardening, say, in America

indicators.note: say signals that the phrase is spoken and heard as something else

parts.note: observed is eyed, and one tool employed in gardening is a hoe: eyed a hoe

explanation.surface: Watching someone at work in an American garden.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken quickly, 'eyed a hoe' runs together into the name of the western US state.
explanation.definitionFit: Idaho is a state of the USA, so it lies within the country.

clue.text: "Go, for they call you. from the hill" (M.Arnold)

definitions.text: "Go, for they call you. from the hill" (M.Arnold)

parts.words: "Go, for they call you. from the hill" (M.Arnold)
parts.note: the opening line of Matthew Arnold's poem The Scholar-Gipsy has a missing word addressed to a keeper of flocks

explanation.surface: A line of Victorian verse with a gap to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: The missing word is the addressee in the first line of Matthew Arnold's The Scholar-Gipsy.
explanation.definitionFit: Arnold's poem opens by addressing a flock keeper in the Oxford hills.

clue.text: Non-committal stance, upright on horseback

definitions.meaning: taking both sides, sitting on the fence
sitting with a leg on each side, astride a mount

explanation.surface: A rider sitting tall but refusing to take sides.
explanation.definitionFit: To bestride is to sit with legs either side, and figuratively to back both sides of an argument.

clue.text: Where Hawke rated somehow as a rebel

indicators.note: somehow says the letters are arranged in some other way

explanation.surface: Asking how a man named Hawke came to be ranked as a rebel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Somehow' rearranges all fifteen letters of WHERE HAWKE RATED.
explanation.definitionFit: Hereward was the Anglo-Saxon leader who resisted the Norman conquest from the Fens.

clue.text: Acquire a letter from Lucian to a lady

parts.note: Lucian wrote in Greek, and chi is a Greek letter
Eve, the first woman, is a stock lady

explanation.surface: Obtaining a letter written by the satirist Lucian to a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Lucian was a Greek satirist, so a letter from him is a letter of the Greek alphabet, not a piece of correspondence.
explanation.definitionFit: To achieve something is to gain or attain it through effort.

clue.text: Old capital hostile to sur-. prise announcement by the Scots

parts.note: anti means opposed to

parts.words: sur-. prise announcement by the Scots
parts.note: och is a Scottish exclamation of surprise or regret

explanation.surface: An ancient seat of power resisting a startling Scottish declaration.
explanation.walkthrough: The stray hyphen and full stop in 'sur-. prise' are line-break debris from the page; read 'surprise'.
explanation.definitionFit: Antioch was the capital of the Seleucid empire and of Roman Syria.

clue.text: Wheeler's find, perhaps, preserves animals

parts.note: to pot food is to preserve it
a herd is a group of animals

explanation.surface: A cyclist or carter discovering a jar of preserved meat.
explanation.walkthrough: Wheeler is Sir Mortimer Wheeler, the archaeologist, not a cyclist or wheelwright; his digs turn up shards of pottery.
explanation.definitionFit: A shard of broken pottery is a typical archaeological dig discovery.

clue.text: Forgiveness makes former copper squeal

definitions.note: a noun; the answer is a verbal noun, the act of pardoning

parts.note: ex means former
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
to squeal on someone, to inform, is to sing

explanation.surface: An ex-policeman winning pardon by informing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' looks like a policeman but gives the chemical symbol; 'squeal' is criminal slang for informing.
explanation.definitionFit: Pardoning a fault is letting someone off, the act of forgiving.

clue.text: Some are curious enough to come round again

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Inquisitive people return for another look.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'enough to come round again' as the definition; 'enough to' is a link, as RECUR means only 'come round again'.
explanation.definitionFit: To recur is to happen again, returning periodically.

clue.text: His scaly members about right for a state of transition?

indicators.note: about says the letters are turned around into a new order

explanation.surface: A creature's scaly limbs suit it for a period of change.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' rearranges HIS SCALY with R; 'members' just joins the clue's surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The pupa stage sits between caterpillar and butterfly, a form in transition.

clue.text: Bishop takes gold to oarsman — not the owner

parts.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
or is gold in heraldry
an oarsman is a rower

explanation.surface: A churchman handing gold to a rower who has no claim to it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has the use of a thing lent to them does not possess it.

clue.text: County town once said to produce material for caulking

indicators.note: said means the place name is heard rather than written

parts.note: Oakham was the county town of Rutland, a county abolished in 1974

explanation.surface: An old county town being credited with producing ship-sealing stuff.
explanation.walkthrough: Oakham was the county town of Rutland, England's smallest county, which ceased to exist in 1974; hence 'once'.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose tarred fibre was hammered into the seams of wooden ships to seal them.

clue.text: One with an exalted calling in Islam?

definitions.text: One with an exalted calling in Islam?

parts.words: One with an exalted calling in Islam?
parts.note: exalted is literal, high up a minaret, and calling is the summons to prayer

explanation.surface: A holy man with a lofty vocation in the Muslim faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exalted calling' suggests a noble vocation, but it means calling out from a height.
explanation.definitionFit: The mosque official cries the call to prayer from the top of a minaret.

clue.text: Make a lot of noise about engineers going round a butter factory

indicators.note: the word for making noise is placed about everything else

parts.note: to cry is to shout loudly

indicators.note: going round means the engineers enclose the next letter

parts.note: REME is the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers, a British army corps

explanation.surface: Raising a din about army engineers touring a dairy plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going round' wraps the engineers round A, making REAME; 'about' then puts the noise word round all of that. REME is a British army corps.
explanation.definitionFit: A dairy where milk is processed into cream and cheese is a creamery.

clue.text: Virtuoso from Miss West's centre in Detroit

parts.note: Mae West was the American film actress

indicators.note: the centre letters of the city's name are taken, dropping each end

explanation.surface: A star performer emerging from Mae West's home base in Motor City.
explanation.walkthrough: Miss West's is MAE'S, giving MAES; the centre of DETROIT without its outer letters gives TRO.
explanation.definitionFit: A maestro is a master performer or conductor.

clue.text: Mount an attack on a southern ship

parts.note: a sail stands for a ship, as in 'a fleet of fifty sail'

explanation.surface: Launching a raid on a vessel from the south.
explanation.definitionFit: To assail is to attack violently.

clue.text: Quell leaders of revolt endangering the fourth estate

indicators.note: leaders are the opening letters of the next two words

parts.note: the press is called the fourth estate

explanation.surface: Putting down a rebellion's chiefs who threaten journalists.
explanation.definitionFit: To repress is to put down or subdue.

clue.text: Look among part of the audience for a guide

indicators.note: the word for look goes among the letters of the other piece

parts.note: the pit is the area of a theatre where some audience sits
lo means look, behold

explanation.surface: Searching the stalls for someone to show the way.
explanation.definitionFit: A pilot steers ships into harbour, showing the way.

clue.text: They are on the wicket, and may be popping

definitions.text: They are on the wicket, and may be popping

parts.words: They are on the wicket, and may be popping
parts.note: cricket pitch lines include the popping one where the batsman stands

explanation.surface: Things on a cricket pitch that might suddenly burst.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the lines marked on the pitch near the stumps include the popping one, behind which the batsman is safe.
explanation.definitionFit: Cricket's marked white lines near each set of stumps bear that name.

clue.text: Had no future as a literary sketch

parts.note: the phrase had no future paraphrases came to nothing, so had stands for came
no future is nothing ahead, the round zero letter

explanation.surface: A short piece of writing whose subject had no prospects.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Had no future' is read as 'came to nothing': CAME, then O for nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A cameo is a short vivid piece of writing or character portrait.

clue.text: Digger's noted way of carrying the swag

definitions.text: Digger's noted way of carrying the swag

parts.words: Digger's noted way of carrying the swag
parts.note: an Australian swagman's tramping with his bedroll, famous in song

explanation.surface: An Australian's well-known method of humping his bundle.
explanation.walkthrough: A Digger is an Australian; 'noted' means set to music, the bush ballad about a swagman; the swag is his bedroll, not loot.
explanation.definitionFit: Australian slang for tramping with a swag, also the title of the famous bush ballad.

clue.text: Reprimand for the class

explanation.surface: A teacher scolding a whole form.
explanation.definitionFit: A rating is both a dressing-down and a classification by grade.

clue.text: Business deficit a pound? Hardly to be described thus

parts.note: co is short for company
a loss is a deficit
L is the abbreviation for pound, from libra

explanation.surface: A company down by just a pound would hardly call it huge.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition comments on the wordplay: a business deficit of a pound could hardly be described as enormous.
explanation.definitionFit: A shortfall of one pound is tiny, so calling it immense would be absurd.
